column1: # title: ENG-205 Middle Ages Intro — 2 Names

column2: Honorius was the Roman emperor who recalled the troops from Britain in AD 410. That left the Britons defenseless, as the video on Roman to Anglo-Saxon Britain explains.

Alfred the Great, who reigned from 871 to 899, was the first true English king, and he united the kingdoms against the Danes. He created the fyrd, written law, a fleet, the Witan and the shires, and he commissioned the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. He also supported Latin learning and Bede's Ecclesiastical History.
Bede was a monk who completed the Ecclesiastical History of the English People in 731. It is our main source for the period, and it contains Caedmon's Hymn.
Caedmon was an illiterate cowherd who became a poet. His Caedmon's Hymn, from around 658 to 680, is the earliest poem recorded in English.
Edward the Confessor was the Anglo-Saxon king who built Westminster Abbey. He died childless in 1066, which triggered the fight over who would succeed him.
Harold Godwinson was the Earl of Wessex, and the Witan chose him as king in 1066. He lost the crown to William at the Battle of Hastings.

William the Conqueror, also called William I, was the Duke of Normandy who led the Norman Conquest in 1066 and ruled until 1087. He put a French-speaking ruling class in power, gave land to Norman vassals, built 5,000 to 6,000 castles and ordered the Domesday Survey. He also made all landholders swear loyalty to him.
Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote the History of the Kings of Britain in Latin around 1135 to 1138. It is the source of the Arthurian legends.
Marie de France wrote the Lais, around 1165 to 1180, in Anglo-Norman French. She drew them from Breton sources.

The Gawain poet, also called the Pearl poet, is the anonymous author of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, written around 1375 to 1400. The poem belongs to the Alliterative Revival and survives in only one manuscript.

Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in Middle English around 1387 to 1399, mostly in rhymed couplets with five-stress lines, and he also wrote Troilus and Criseyde. As the son of a wine merchant, he stands for the rising merchant class.
William Langland wrote Piers Plowman between 1377 and 1379. It is an alliterative dream vision that criticizes society and the Church after the plague, and it describes the July 'hungry gap'.
John Wycliffe was a reformer who attacked corruption in the Church. His followers, the Lollards, began the first complete English Bible around 1380.
Julian of Norwich wrote the Book of Showings between 1373 and 1393. It is a Christian visionary text, part of the important fourteenth-century trend of Christian visionary writing.
Margery Kempe is the author of The Book of Margery Kempe, which she wrote around 1432 to 1438.
Sir Thomas Malory wrote Le Morte Darthur in prison around 1470. It is the great prose collection of Arthurian romance, and William Caxton printed it in 1485.
William Caxton set up England's first printing press in 1476. His moveable type made fast, identical copies possible, and he printed Malory's Morte Darthur in 1485.

Henry VII, also called Henry Tudor, won the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485 and married Elizabeth of York, ending the Wars of the Roses. He began the Tudor dynasty, which is where the Middle Ages end.
Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries in the 1530s. That ended their role as England's main producers of books.
